That the government cease its present efforts to downgrade the role of the monarchy in Canada and, instead, give strong support to the Queen and the royal family as they carry out their duties with such dignity and effectiveness.

subsubtopic: ACTION TO BE TAKEN AGAINST ILLEGAL STRIKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. The minister stated yesterday he would not elaborate as to specific courses of action he might take in connection with the illegal activities of a minority of workers in the postal services. However, Canadians are wondering for how long we can allow a double standard to continue with regard to a majority of law-abiding labour and a minority of law-defying labour.
Could the minister advise the House, if not specifically, what the government intends to do, bearing in mind the legislation passed earlier this week, the present status of the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the provisions of the Criminal Code, under the options available to it by way of injunctions, dismissal or other form of recourse? Surely the public is entitled to know that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: ACTION TO BE TAKEN AGAINST ILLEGAL STRIKERS
speechtext:
The hon. member has mentioned the options that are available. It might be noted that even in a case like this in regard to which parliament passed a law very recently, it is still necessary to gather the facts and move with care when proceeding against individuals. It is our intention to do that, to ensure that the law is respected.
I said the other day, and I say again, that respect for the law comes best through ordinary compliance with the law by Canadian citizens, and I make a plea again to the individuals involved and their friends that that point be noted and be made time and time again. In the current circumstances we are proceeding, and the first action to be taken is proceeding by way of seeking injunctions. That material is being prepared, and that may be in court this afternoon in certain localities.

subtopic: SUGGESTED MEETING WITH CUPW TO STOP ILLEGAL PICKETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Justice defined very well the steps he intends to take with regard to legal procedures. I want to reiterate what I said yesterday, that is that if they come to work at any post office in Canada, they will be paid. subsubtopic: RIGHT OF PROVINCES TO COLLECT INDIRECT TAXES IN RESOURCE AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister: it arises out of the very important decision that was reached by the Supreme Court of Canada in the Cigol case. As the Prime Minister will know, the decision reached by the Supreme Court declared ultra vires the law passed by the government of Saskatchewan which it thought was very clearly within its jurisdictional authority.
While considering that constitutional control of resources, the right to have effective management over resources, means something to the provinces-in this respect I am thinking specifically of forests, mines and minerals-would the Prime Minister agree that the law should make it perfectly clear that provincial governments have the right to levy indirect taxes in these fields?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: RESOURCES
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF PROVINCES TO COLLECT INDIRECT TAXES IN RESOURCE AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me remind the leader of the NDP that as far back as 1969 we had proposed constitutional changes which would permit provinces to levy indirect taxes. The only proviso was that that did not affect interprovincial or international trade. It is obvious that only the federal government can have jurisdiction to regulate international trade-if Canada is, indeed, to be a country-and no province should be able to use the tax method to prevent free trade across Canada. These are the two provisos that we put then, and we still stand by them.
The Supreme Court made a very simple judgment: it is that the province indeed was trying to use powers it did not have in order to regulate international trade. We think the Supreme Court made a decision which stands on its own merit, and I am somewhat surprised that the leader of the NDP is trying now, across the House by way of a question, to suggest that Canada should not continue to exercise the power to regulate the common market within Canada.

subtopic: RESOURCES
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF PROVINCES TO COLLECT INDIRECT TAXES IN RESOURCE AREAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: RESOURCES
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF PROVINCES TO COLLECT INDIRECT TAXES IN RESOURCE AREAS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister knows very well that at least on this matter I and my party are in basic agreement with him: the federal authority must remain very strong indeed to ensure that there is an equitable distribution of the benefits of the wealth, for example, that occur throughout this country. The federal government has the right to levy its own indirect taxes on resources.
In his letter to the Prime Minister dated October 10, 1978, Premier Blakeney requested that the provinces be given at least the same right exclusively in the field of resources, and I have named the three areas of resources. That was accepted unanimously by the ten provinces in 1976; also, I thought it was accepted by the federal government. If the Prime Minister is in agreement with that, will he follow it up at the upcoming

first ministers' conference and accept the suggestion of making an amendment to the Constitution of Canada to remove all uncertainty in this area?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: RESOURCES
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF PROVINCES TO COLLECT INDIRECT TAXES IN RESOURCE AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party said that he supported my view in so far as it permitted the redistribution of wealth across Canada. That is not the case I am making. Of course we must have that power. We have it now, and we exercise it.
I am making another case, that no province should be able to use its jurisdiction to prevent the free flow of goods across provincial borders. That is why, in the area of indirect taxation which can be used for this purpose, we stand by the position we have always taken and we think the position of the court is correct.
In 1976, Premier Blakeney reached some position on resources. We will debate that at the end of the month. We hope some accommodation is possible. We want provinces to be able to exercise fully their jurisdiction over resources, but when there is a conflicting interest with the importance of maintaining within Canada the free flow of goods, whether they be resources, manufactured products or anything else, then we think the federal government should remain supreme-and that is the position we will take.

If that can be done, it will take some of the pressure of moving Saskatchewan grain away from the movement of Manitoba grain, allowing Manitoba grain to move more freely to Thunder Bay. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice: it is supplementary to questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
It seems to me there is a little foot-dragging here. The minister indicated that he wants to get the facts. The facts are that we have an illegal strike and illegal picketing. It seems to me that the minister has admitted there are three options: an injunction, criminal proceedings, and dismissal.
I want to know what makes the minister think an injunction is going to work, when in fact we know there is a small group that is defying the law at this particular time. Why does the minister opt for an injunction at this time? What are the reasons for moving for an injunction at this urgent moment, rather than spelling out why he has not sought proceedings under the Criminal Code, or dismissal? I think he must explain that.

Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that all the options were being examined and there are different timeframes for each of them. Hon. members may think that a law, having been passed, it can be enforced against individuals automatically. That is not the case. The Attorney General labours under the difficulty that he still must respect the civil liberties of people and still must respect due process. It is a difficulty I labour under very gladly, I may say, because I do not believe that generalizations can lead to criminality or conviction. That simply does not work in our country, either. When I talk about the respect for the law that I want these individuals to observe, I think it is partly because we carefully observe these traditions, that the law does, indeed, deserve that respect.
I should make it clear that the injunctions referred to and which we will be seeking will be directly related to the picketing activity which, of course, is an obstacle to the resumption of work by those who do, indeed, want to go back to work. That is a first step and one which we hope we can take as quickly as possible. I cannot comment on that further, again because of traditions about what one should say in respect of what will be going before the courts.
As far as other matters are concerned, the facts in relation to individuals and in relation to the law are being obtained and further action will be taken. I do not say that in any sense of trying to hold out a threat, because I fall back again on my original statement, that willingness to obey the law and the recognition of that principle is of most fundamental importance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would have more faith in the minister's answer if he had taken the opportunity to give me and the people of Canada some indication as to what he was referring to in terms of timeframes.

speechtext: My question, Mr. Speaker, is to the Minister of Transport. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: TRANSPORT

October 20, 1978

indicated that a consultant analysis had been started in relation to the lengthening of the Seaway season.
The Seaway, under current circumstances, is likely to be approaching its full capacity in a fairly short period of time-a very short period of years. USE OF CHURCHILL IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is supplementary to the questions of the hon. member for Lisgar: it is to the Minister of Transport. When the minister said that alternate routes for shipping grain out of Canada for export would be looked at, he failed to mention the port of Churchill.
I would like to ask the minister if he would give consideration to my suggestion, that when the m.v. Arctic comes into Churchill on November 15, because it is a class II icebreaker it be accompanied by four or five other ships, thus bringing the shipping of grain out of Churchill up to the anticipated 30 million bushels?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: USE OF CHURCHILL IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not mention the port of Churchill for the very good reason that for the last four or five years we have been maximizing, absolutely, to the highest extent possible, the volume of grain moving through Churchill. Therefore, we can add nothing more to it under current circumstances.
The problem with shipping into Churchill late in the season may have just been emphasized, and that is the difficulty with ice which the m.v. Arctic has just run into. In view of that difficulty, I am not at all sure at this point in time if it will be able to make the trip which originally had been planned. I do say, however, that the fact this ice-strengthened vessel ran into difficulty is some indication in logic to the hon. member as to why other vessels may not want to try the trip at that time of year. The solution to Churchill's problem may lie more in lengthening the season by avoiding certain ice problems in the harbour, but they are not simple problems to overcome.

subtopic: USE OF CHURCHILL IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the solution to the problems in Churchill would be the changing of this government. The minister said that the port of Churchill was being utilized to its full capacity. I believe he has read the Bryden report and not the Hall commission report which says that 55 million bushels could be shipped through this port.
In light of that, will the minister now take it upon himself to ask the Wheat Board, if they cannot ship another 4 million or 5 million bushels out of Churchill, if in fact they will store the cargo which has been sold for shipment out of Churchill, next year in Churchill, thus easing the pressure on storage facilities on the prairies?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: USE OF CHURCHILL IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the existing situation allows railway cars to be available, the Wheat Board may well find it
Oral Questions
possible to move grain into storage in Churchill earlier than they had anticipated. That does depend, however, on whether cars can be freed from the other movements of grain.
As far as the question of expanding the port of Churchill to handle 55 million bushels is concerned, the Hall commission report recommended the construction of a very expensive terminal inland in order to accomplish that. I have to say that, looking at this from the point of view of total economic benefits, it is still true that the placing of that terminal at Prince Rupert where it could be used 12 months of the year, or at Thunder Bay where it could be used nine or ten months, simply gets a lot more grain through for the dollars available.
I hope the hon. member will appreciate that, even as a westerner who has long and strongly worked for the port of Churchill and its development, I too have to take into account the use of those dollars and the fact that if you can get two or three times the grain through for the same expenditure, then it would be something in the way of a waste to not do it in that fashion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice in his capacity as Attorney General. In the Senate, on October 18, 1978, with respect to the postal matters, Senator van Roggen wanted to know whether or not there was sufficient provision in the Public Service Staff Relations Act to enable the Minister of Labour to terminate the employment of those who disobey the law, as opposed to only fining them. There have been press reports which say that a search of that act has indicated that the power does not rest there.
With respect to the remedies which are available to the Government of Canada, and in view of that uncertainty, can the Attorney General assure the House that the government has the capacity to dismiss for failure to obey the law, if that should be a remedy that the government would consider? subsubtopic: JAPANESE INVESTMENT IN WEST COAST SHIPPING-EFFECT ON FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It concerns the very substantial investment by Japanese interests in the west coast shipping industry and the potential that this will have an adverse effect in terms of employment, pricing and processing of fish.
My question is: what steps has the minister taken to see that Canadian capital is available for west coast fishing interests, rather than Japanese capital of foreign capital, so that we can be assured that we are moving in the direction of Canadian ownership in terms of our west coast fisheries, rather than in the direction we are now, which is toward a foreign-dominated west coast fishery?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: JAPANESE INVESTMENT IN WEST COAST SHIPPING-EFFECT ON FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to Canadian ownership of the west coast fishing industry, any new venture by Japanese capital, or any other capital, into starting a new business in British Columbia, naturally would have to go through FIRA. Any takeover would have to go through FIRA. With regard to funds available from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, it might be of interest to know that the Federal Business Development Bank last year loaned approximately $479 million and one-quarter of that money went to British Columbia.
In my own department, the enterprise development program was recently approved by Treasury Board to insure up to $1 billion in loans. I have said many times in this House that last year we helped 256 companies and that all but 7 of those companies were Canadian-owned. So we have money available and are prepared to assist any industry that can bring forward a bona fide case and show that it is particularly interested in developing the fishing industry, or any other industry.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: JAPANESE INVESTMENT IN WEST COAST SHIPPING-EFFECT ON FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister fails to tell us how much of that money went into the fishing industry. I can tell him that it was miniscule. Under the foreign investment review mechanism, only takeovers are reviewed. What is happening is that we have Japanese interests that are putting up loan capital rather that equity capital, and are therefore getting in under the review mechanism. This means that when you have tied contracts in terms of products, where you have a foreign company that is able to tie up your products because of a loan rather than a purchase, that is not reviewable.
My question is: will the minister now consider changing the provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act so that these

kinds of product agreements which are coming in through the back door-through loan, rather than equity-will be reviewable?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: JAPANESE INVESTMENT IN WEST COAST SHIPPING-EFFECT ON FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to look at all possible suggestions to facilitate Canadian business; but the hon. member is quite wrong when he suggests that only takeovers are reviewed by the Foreign Investment Review Agency. New businesses are also under review by the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
With regard to the Federal Business Development Bank, as I said, one quarter of the money loaned last year was loaned in British Columbia, and one-quarter loaned last year was in manufacturing. I will have to see how much went into the fishing industry. But the initiative must rest with the private sector; they must come to the bank and ask for a loan.

speechtext: They are on strike.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It arises from remarks made in this House yesterday by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin). The parliamentary secretary, unintentionally I assume, misled the House when he said, referring to myself:
The hon. member knows this. He knows authority is being obtained now to cover the government's needs not only for the balance of the present fiscal year but for the next fiscal year so as to avoid our having to come back to parliament time and time again for the necessary legislation if we are to meet the expenditures which he himself, along with other members of the finance committee, examined in detail when the estimates were before the committee last spring and supported there.
My point of order is twofold. First, the current year's estimates as they were before our committee, and indeed in this House, were opposed on many points and, to the limit of our procedural ability, we tried to have certain of these estimates defeated.
My main point of order is that for the parliamentary secretary to suggest that expenditures for the next fiscal year, fiscal 1980, have already been approved, is totally erroneous. We have not seen the figures. We have seen no estimates. Indeed, we have seen no indication, even in the form of a budget, as to what the government plans for 1980 as far as expenditures are concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, toward the end of my remarks last night I was talking about the town of Churchill and the recreational complex which was built there by the government at a cost of some $13 million, and the fact that there are only 1,400 people left in this community which is saddled with keeping this huge complex in operation.
For some time I have been trying to establish what could be done with this white elephant, as it must be called at this time. I have heard some rumblings, some rumours, that a university

of the north might be in the offing-I understand the government is in something of a dilemma with regard to this complex. I suggest that consideration be given to setting up a university of the north in Churchill for postgraduate work in engineering, scientific research, and so on. Those studying there could concentrate on the potential of the north, not only in Manitoba but in Canada generally.
At present most of our northern research is carried out in places far removed from the north and it is about time that the government, having created this monster, seriously considered establishing a new university in the north for postgraduate work. Churchill is well known for its involvement in scientific work of various kinds and this huge complex could become the hub of such a university as I am proposing.
At the beginning of my speech I mentioned Otineka and Le Pas and the billion dollar loan to Panama. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that north of the 53rd parallel in Manitoba, Liberal words about restraint have an odd ring to them. In 1970 the Le Pas Indian band, a group of approximately 1,200 Cree-speaking people, made a proposal for a small shopping complex to be built on their reserve. What they had in mind was a complex covering some 25,000 square feet. The proposal was accepted by the federal government through the minister of Indian affairs at that time, now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). What did the people of Le Pas end up with? It is hard to believe. The Indians wanted a little store. Ottawa built them a mall. Once approval had been given by the minister, work went ahead and, by the time the mall was completed, it covered 190,000 square feet. The estimated cost was in the neighbourhood of $4 million, and the final cost was $8.4 million. I attempted several times in committee to ascertain the reasons for this huge cost overrun. Invariably I was told that it was due to government overbilling.
I will tell you what happened, Mr. Speaker. The Indians have been placed in a most difficult position because once the mall had been built the government turned it over to the band organization; Harry Wilson, the chairman of the Otineka corporation, is finding it almost impossible to make it a paying proposition, although he is working very hard, for the simple reason that this 190,000 square feet mall is still not filled though the complex was officially opened two years ago. As a result the government has felt obliged to write off $4.2 million of the guaranteed loan it gave in connection with this mall.
The Indian people have been put in the position of trying to bail the government out of a situation it manufactured for itself by allowing spending to get completely out of control. It is the taxpayers of Canada who are being called upon to pay the $4.2 million the government wrote off some two months ago, and if things continue as they are now in that shopping mall, the government will be spending still more of the taxpayers' dollars to write off the entire debt. I would like to develop this theme further but I am sure it is not new to hon. members. It is just another example of the bumbling mismanagement and overspending that have gone on under this government. These things happen because the government decides to take matters out of the hands of the communities concerned. Costly
October 20, 1978

gifts are made, and then they walk away from them, declining responsibility for upkeep and maintenance once the initial construction has been completed.
What does the bill before us ask parliament to do? The government is seeking authority to borrow another $17 billion, and I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I shall want some answers from the minister before I agree to it. For example, is $1 billion of that $17 billion going to the Republic of Panama for the development of a copper mine there as the EDC is planning right now? The EDC was, of course, somewhat embarrassed when General Torrijos announced in a speech in Panama that Canada has agreed to guarantee a $1 billion loan to that country to help develop the Cerro Colorado mine. EDC denied this, however, stating that negotiations for the loan were still at an early stage.
On October 16 I learned that this loan had still not been guaranteed and that the final negotiations had not been completed. However, it is the intention of the government to go ahead, and the EDC says it is a very good project in which to get involved. But how do I explain to the miner at the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company at Flin Flon, which mines copper and zinc, that we have a government which is taking tax dollars and sending them to the Republic of Panama to develop a copper mine there? The miner at Flin Flon is wondering if he will be laid off next week because the Canadian copper industry has gone to rock bottom. How do I explain that? There is no way.
What the government should be doing with this $1 billion it is considering lending to the Republic of Panama is putting it into the Canadian mining industry, so that instead of shipping raw materials to other parts of the world and buying back manufactured goods, that $1 billion should go into the Canadian mining industry so it can process raw materials here and provide much needed jobs.
Hon. members opposite can smile, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) can say that the Churchill constituency receives a bigger grant under the Canada Works Program than any other constituency, but that does not satisfy me, because that constituency has the highest rate of unemployment. Churchill is entitled to a bigger grant if money is going to be handed out in that fashion. We need long-term jobs, but lending $1 billion to the Republic of Panama to develop another copper mine will certainly not provide jobs in Canada. That money should be used to develop processing right here in Canada.
The chamber of commerce of Leaf Rapids, Manitoba, has sent a petition to the government. The chamber of commerce of Thompson, Manitoba, sent a petition to the government telling it to get off this foolishness. Instead of financing a copper mine in the Republic of Panama, why not put some money into the sagging mining industry right here in Canada? The government is asking for authority to borrow another $17 billion, but I certainly will not vote for this bill unless we know where this money is going to be spent.
Borrowing Authority Act
I am dealing only with the Churchill constituency. Will some of this money be spent on another white elephant complex in Churchill? Will it be spent to built another huge shopping mall like the one which has become an empty barn in northern Manitoba? Will it be used to send another $1 billion to the Republic of Panama?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate and to make a few points which I think are rather essential when we are talking about the national debt and its relative size in terms of the gross national product.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) made an interesting speech in the House yesterday dealing with some new economics and dealing with what he termed a new society. I have talked about this three or four times in this House, and I will say it again and again-there were very important lessons to learn from the hon. member's speech, and I have some other thoughts along the same line, that is, that there is no question that in the world today a whole range of industrial nations are undergoing some very serious economic problems.
Japan has a surplus of trade, and therefore a yen which is very high. Japan is finding it more and more difficult to compete with dollars like ours. West Germany and Switzerland, which have relatively low inflation rates, still have some very serious long-term problems. The IMF and the Big Seven talk in terms of 5 per cent as being like zero in relation to inflation. It is not like it used to be when 2 per cent was considered normal. We now have to deal with figures like that.
Unemployment is a problem throughout the world; much more so in Canada than in most other countries, but it is certainly a problem throughout the world. There are many social problems which are being faced by all countries.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge said that ours is a new society. I prefer the term "new economics". There is a totally new notion called scarcity, and we find this in the major area of energy. This has some very major ramifications for the world's governments. The net outflow of about $50 billion a year to the Arab countries from the United States is one of those ramifications, and it has militated considerably against the economy of the United States and the American dollar. Because of our reliance in terms of trade upon the United States, there are ramifications for our economy as well.
We are told that we must expect to spend about $180 billion over the next 15 or 20 years on energy projects. That amount far exceeds the rate at which we are spending today. That rate

October 20, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
more than doubles the number of capital dollars going into energy projects in relation to the total number of capital dollars available.
Another factor which seems to be little known to hon. members opposite is that the techniques which have served us well in the past, Keynesian fiscal and monetary techniques, are no longer working the way they did, and for two reasons. One is the nature and size of the problem. It is interesting to hear members of the Conservative party talking about $2 billion in tax relief as the kind of stimulus which will really move things. This is what the Tories plan to do if they happen to be fortunate enough, from their point of view, or unfortunate enough, from the point of view of the country, to be in power.
They talk about a $2 billion tax cut changing things. That is the same figure we used to hear in the early sixties. We were told that such a move would change the economy around and move things along. In those days we were talking about a gross national product of $40 billion to $50 billion. Today we are talking about a gross national product of $220 billion. We were talking about a stimulus of 4 per cent or 5 per cent at that time, and now we are talking about a stimulus of .75 per cent to 1 per cent, and saying that that will move the economy. I want to talk about that later, but at this point I am saying that the magnitude of the problems make it almost impossible for this to happen.
Present techniques also tend to be counter-productive. That is the thing which worries most economists. This was mentioned by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge. He said that if there were tax cuts to stimulate growth in the economy, we could expect that money to go into savings. Back in the early sixties about 2 per cent or 2.3 per cent of the gross national product went into savings. Today the figure is about 10 per cent, a growth factor of about 4. This goes into savings and therefore does not get into the stream as purchasing power. Some goes in terms of purchasing luxury goods, which often means that money flows out of the country through foreign purchases. People do take trips south and so forth, and while that is desirable from an individual point of view, it is not the kind of thing which stimulates the Canadian economy.
I am using this to illustrate the point that these techniques do not work the way they used to work, and some of them are counterproductive. For instance, there is a good case to be made that if you do in fact increase the deficit by a tax cut, the increased deficit will have an effect on inflation. Increased inflationary costs will mean that our goods cost more and more on the world market, and very often that might mean that we produce less and there are fewer jobs. It used to be that if you had a little inflation, you would have few unemployed. There is a case to be made today for actually increasing unemployment by increasing inflation.
So, putting these factors together, I think we are going into a new economic world, and some of the things we are saying in the House do not work any more. I think that was the case that the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge made, and that

is the case that many of us on both sides of the House have been making. We have to look at new ways of handling our economic problems.
When we come to Canada more specifically, we have one or two unique problems which separate our efforts from the efforts of other countries to solve their economic problems. The most compelling single factor that makes us very different from any of the other OECD countries is the high rate of unemployment and, more basically, the very large growth in our labour force.
I have used these figures before, but I will use them again because I think we must keep saying this. I have a chart in front of me from Statistics Canada which was produced in spring. If one takes the year 1965 as the base year, using the figure 100, one finds that for every 100 persons in the labour force in West Germany in 1965 there is now something in the order of 96 or 97 people, an actual decline of people in the labour force; for every 100 people in the labour force in Italy in 1965, there is still 100; for every 100 in the United Kingdom, there is about 104 now; Sweden has about 112; France, 110; Japan, about 114. All of these are major countries with which we can compare ourselves.
Let us not compare ourselves with Mauritius or some such country with which it is not possible to compare economies. Let us compare our economy with those of the Big Seven and the major European countries, the economies of which are similar to ours. Taking them as a kind of average, you find that most of those countries have had either no growth in their labour force or a growth of perhaps less than 10 people per 100 over the period from 1965 to the end of 1977.
There are three countries that stand out beyond these figures. One of them is the United States, which has 28 more people per 100 in the labour force than they had in 1965, and one is Australia, which has 30 more people per 100 in the labour force than they had in 1965. This is quite different from the first group. But there is one country that stands out in a way that no other does, and that is Canada. We had 46 more people per 100 in the labour force at the end of last year than we did in 1965, way above anyone else. Even with an 8.5 per cent or 9 per cent, or even a 10 per cent unemployment rate in this country-and there is always a debate about this rate-we would not have a really serious problem in this country, having done the things we have done to create jobs, if we had at this stage the same growth in the labour force that exists in the United States. That is the fundamental difference between Canada and the other countries to which I referred. The growth in our labour force has been unbelievable.
This is what concerns me in the House. I hear people saying, "Throw another $2 billion into the hopper, and we will solve the problem". The NDP member would up the ante to about $4 billion. This is an horrendous problem. We have 46 more people in the labour force per 100 than there were 12 years ago.
Why am I talking about this when we are talking about our national debt and the money we need to cover it? I am talking about it specifically because this growth in the labour force
October 20, 1978

has been the single factor that has created the problems which have brought us this debt. We have a massive $4.5 billion to $5 billion going out in UIC payments each year. This is entirely related to the growth in the labour force. I haven't the figures at hand at this point, but several billion dollars have gone out to DREE, in transfer payments to provinces, to Canada Works, and so on. All this is entirely related to the growth in the labour force.
I do not think I am exaggerating one iota when I say-it is probably absolutely true-that if our labour force growth was like the growth in the U.S. labour force, we would be incurring virtually no debt today simply because we would not have to spend that money. I would say we could wipe out $10 billion to $12 billion of government expenditures if we had the same situation that exists in the United States, given what we have done in the past. I think there is much nonsense being said in the House and in the press that totally ignores that fact.
If you pick up the Globe and Mail or any other newspaper, you often find on the first page some statement about the economy which is totally isolated from the context, like the statement I heard this morning on the CBC credited to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) that our national debt has increased four or five times over the last 15 or 20 years and that his is a very bad situation. This is the kind of thing the public keeps hearing.
If you turn to the financial page of the Globe and Mail, of the Financial Post, or of most of the larger newspapers, you will find a slightly different story. They will not be saying that the growth in our debt has increased four or five times. They will say, yes, it is four or five times larger, but also the GNP has grown four or five times. Actually, we have somewhat less debt as related to the GNP today than we had 15 years ago. This is what one finds in the financial pages of the papers and this is what economists tell me; this is what I find when I read various economic journals. But when I read the front pages of our daily newspapers, all I see are these alarming, disturbing figures. Now we have reached the point where the press, the opposition, and the government have to talk about real figures. They have to talk about the real growth in the labour force and the effect of that real growth on our economy.
So I am saying-and I have been saying it all along but I hope that perhaps I am saying it better now because it takes some time to understand this-along with the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge-and I do not agree with all his solutions-that we have a new economics now, a new set of problems which will not be solved by the simplistic, Keynesian techniques that were used in the past. They were great in the 1960s; they do not obtain today.
Now I should like to spend a couple of minutes talking about some of my concerns in terms of the things the opposition members have been saying in what I think are their honest efforts-in no way am I imputing to someone dishonesty in this business-to find solutions to our economic problems. It is not dishonesty. It is that people have not come to grips with the fact that there is an essential qualitative change in the world's economies. Canadians are affected by that as much as
Borrowing Authority Act
anyone else. This essential qualitative change is what we should study. I am not talking about dishonesty, misleading information, or anything of that nature. I am talking about government leaders throughout the world not understanding the phenomena referred to by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, myself, and others.
I should like to refer to one of the recent statements of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) regarding mortgage and municipal taxation deductions from income tax. It is not a bad idea. It appeals to a lot of people, even though this type of program contains some grave inequities which must be dealt with. Certainly the government has looked very, very carefully at the same type of program. We see some of the desirability in it. There is no question a lot of middle class people are caught in a bind. This particular suggestion by the opposition makes some sense, so it should not be rejected out of hand. But we should look at it, taking into account the new economics.
I rose today in order to look at these suggestions and so-called techniques, taking into account the world in which we are living. There could not be a worse time to advance a mortgage and taxation refund program. The deficit for this fiscal year is $11 billion or $12 billion, and the opposition comes forth with an idea which would increase the deficit to $14 billion or $15 billion. There has been some mention of figures, but the best figures of many economists indicate an amount of close to $4 billion shared by provincial, federal, and municipal governments.
In view of the inflationary situation, an increased deficit is not acceptable at this particular point. The suggestion of the opposition is a good and valid one, if it is applied to Keynesian economics and the pre-1975 period. The point is that $2 billion, $3 billion or $4 billion is put into the housing sector in the hope of stimulating it and creating jobs. There are a lot of economists in the world who do not believe that $2 billion or $3 billion will result in any material change in the growth of this country. Therefore government revenues will not be increased one iota because of this increased demand. That is why I feel such a proposition is very bad at this particular time. I do not believe it will increase jobs or have any effect on the job market. It will not have the expected effects on revenue. Therefore, it can be only inflationary and further increase the deficit.
The opposition party has claimed for a long time that government spending must be reduced. There are problems with deficits, but government revenues cannot be cut back. An interesting chart was put out by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) which showed revenues and expenditures, side by side, for the last ten years. The lines continued along parallel, and crossed at points which indicated small deficits or surpluses. Suddenly in 1974-75 the expenditure line continued to rise but the revenue line almost flattened. It is not a slow turn; it is an abrupt one. What happened in that period? The then minister of finance, in a minority government, on the
318
October 20, 1978

Borrowing Authority Act
suggestion of a push by the Tory party leader, at one particular point decided to index exemptions. Everything else was indexed, so we indexed exemptions, and the curve went off. The revenue line flattened right out.
One cannot have it both ways. Government deficits cannot be reduced by the reduction of expenditures, if at the same time revenues fall because of decreasing taxes. It will not work, it cannot be done this way. At the present time we are facing a very serious deficit problem. It is inflationary, has a bad effect on the dollar and so on. It is a major problem.
My main criticism of the mortgage and tax deduction notion is that a stimulus of $2 billion, $3 billion or $4 billion in our new economics will not have the same effect as it did in the era of Keynesian economics. It will not have the expected effect. We are talking about a stimulus of perhaps IVi per cent to 2 per cent of the gross national product in total. We are not talking about the effect of a $3 billion or $4 billion stimulus on a $45 billion GNP. We are talking about the effect of an approximate $2 billion stimulus on a $220 billion GNP. It is a very, very small factor, a little over 1 per cent.
The opposition indicated that the mortgage and municipal tax deduction scheme is popular in the United States. Perhaps that is so. One of the very important effects of such a deduction on the United States federal state and municipal taxation system is that more and more taxes are levied on property owners. For example, the average home owner in California is paying in the order of $5,000, $6,000, or $7,000 a year for municipal taxes. If a similar type of situation is placed before our average home owners, one must remember that there is a different kind of problem to face. In the United States this led directly to proposition 13. That was the result of this type of scheme. Property owners are encouraged to keep their homes highly mortgaged, not to pay off existing mortgages, but to remortgage because of these deductions. This is the type of thing which occurred.
The structure of this country supports property owners and property taxes. For example, in my area taxpayers pay approximately $800 or $1,000 a year, as opposed to the $5,000 or $6,000 in California. Of course that $800 or $1,000 is not the total amount of money spent by the municipality. Close to 50 per cent of the money for education in that municipality comes from the provinces. In turn, a lot of that money is transferred from the federal government to the provinces. In a sense we have already a built-in exemption within the federal income tax which is transferred to the provinces for welfare, education, and various purposes not specified. Then it is transferred to the municipalities. This is not the case to any great extent in the United States.
One has to understand these factors, and when you start playing around with the taxation system, making major changes out of the blue a few weeks before a by-election, and when you talk about that kind of change, then you are talking about changing the whole structure we have built up in Canada. I do not say the structure should remain forever

written in stone. The point of the matter is that changing the tax structure is an intricate thing and you do not just pick one little thing out of the hat and say we will do that. We all know that when we take this one small step we are obviously creating all kinds of inequities in terms of those people who now fully own their homes and in terms of those people who rent, and so on. We have to look after those people, and then we start to change the whole tax system.
I do not want to spend much more time on this, but I have dealt with it at some length because in the new economics, and the new kind of thinking that must obtain, there is no room in the future for these kinds of half-baked schemes, of picking something out of the hat, dropping it in and saying we will solve all our problems in this way. In no way do I impute any motive. Rather, I am saying this is the result of not understanding the situation. When a political party picks up something like this and says, "This is how we are going to run the next government," then I do not think that party really has an understanding of what is happening and should not have the right to govern, or that it will really be able to govern under the circumstances.
I really decry partisanship in respect of this kind of thing. When we start looking at the kind of world we are moving toward, the kind of world about which the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge talked, the kind of thing about which I have spoken many times, and about which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has spoken, we must do some new economic thinking about changes that will fit into this new structure. It may well be that a government will be formed by members on the other side at some time in the future. I would ask them, before moving into this kind of thing, to think about the kind of world we are living in, and to avoid coming up with schemes that are good but irrelevant to the times.
Let us talk about a new kind of economics in terms of changes that have occurred and the new approach that must be taken by all nations, Canada included. Let us talk about the fact that we have a massive and unique problem which no other country faces, but which creates all kinds of tensions in this country. I refer to the growth in the labour force. Let us talk about the real terms of this problem rather than giving these $2 billion answers to everything.

Another quotation from the Prime Minister on May 27, 1974, at Etobicoke, Ontario, says, "We are confident that we have a grip on the problem and will wrestle inflation to the ground." That has been quoted before, but apparently inflation wrestled him to the ground. A little later on in that same speech he is quoted as saying, "We are going to bring inflation under control, I pledge you that."
Those quotations are simply part and parcel of a trend through the years in which the Prime Minister has endeavoured to fool the people of Canada into believing that inflation could be controlled. I say this to you: I was prime minister for just less than six years, and the rate of inflation at its highest was 1.2 per cent, the lowest all over the world. We brought in the control of the valuation of money, and we fixed the dollar at 92.5 cents. In consequence this brought to Canada the greatest expansion of trade in its history up to that date.

Why does this government not do something to control the expansion of money? It is because it is easier to permit the expansion than it would be to act with courage and with determination. Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to some of the remarks made concerning this legislation. It seems to me that those who argue that the reason we are borrowing an additional $7 billion is because of waste in government spending, simply do not know what they are talking about and haven't examined any of the fiscal accounts of the Government of Canada.
There is no question the government is in a bind, there is no question that it does not have much choice but to borrow $7 billion, but to say at one side of one's mouth that you can't borrow the $7 billion, and out of the other side, "We are going to allow mortgage deductibility in respect of home ownership and further reduce revenues to the treasury by a major amount", makes no sense whatsoever. There has to be some kind of balance when we consider this question of government waste and government spending.
We have had the experience of the forces of Proposition 13 from California coming into British Columbia and selling the idea that, with a referendum, a simple proposition can be put that says you can cut 20 per cent or 30 per cent of your budget, and still run an efficient and good government. That is a siren song being played in the west and it will probably be played throughout the country. It is the most dangerous kind of proposition I have seen since I became serious about politics.
Just note what has happened. In the city of Berkley, for example, they have shut down their libraries, and they do not have recreational programs.
There is no doubt that we can be more efficient in government. There is no doubt that we can cut a great deal of the fat out of government, but examine the accounts; if you want to start saving money, consider first where you are spending it. The biggest part of the government accounts has to do with health and welfare, child and family allowances, and old age pensions. Yet there is no political party in this House with the courage to get up and say: let us really save money, let us cut $10 from the old age pension. This party would certainly never propose such a thing.
The idea is getting about that somehow or other government spending is bad and private spending is good, that if you build another hamburger stand on the block, that is a wise investment, but if you build a library for your community you are wasting money. That is Milton Friedmanism taken to its logical conclusion. That is the kind of philosophy that is being espoused throughout this country, and it is time the people of Canada took a serious look at the impact of that kind of philosophy in terms of the civilization we have been able to achieve in Canada, one which implies a reasonable balance between public and private spending.

October 20, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
My party will, 1 suspect, vote against this bill because we believe that it is wrong to continue forever with deficit financing. In this particular year we can see a need for additional borrowing, but somewhere along the line we will have to remind ourselves again about what Lord Keynes had to say about budgeting. He still believed that in the long run you had to pay the price. I must say that as a democratic socialist I have just as much objection to deficit budgeting as any right wing Tory. I say to my friends on my left in the Social Credit party that one part of their philosophy that I have always been able to understand-perhaps the only one-is the virtue of balanced budgeting and the virtue of not having a continuing deficit in the accounts.
[DOT] (N42)
We cannot continue to put ourselves in the hands of foreign investors and foreign moneylenders, and as long as we continue to run these kinds of deficits, our capacity for social progress and for flexibility goes down the tubes.
The reality here is that when we have a Sll billion, $12 billion or $13 billion deficit, we can talk all we want about the changes we want to effect in society, but our hands are tied. The hands of this government are tied. If the people of Canada decide to have a Conservative government, the hands of that government will be tied. The hands of a New Democratic Party government would also be tied, because with that kind of deficit there is no room to manoeuvre. There is very little room in which to manoeuvre. Therefore, surely it is in the interests of everyone in this country that we examine the idea of cyclical budgeting rather than having constant deficit financing of $11 billion to $15 billion a year.
The last government in British Columbia, the government of the provincial New Democratic Party, was defeated to a large extent because one of its ministers went $100 million over in his budget. He miscalculated the extent to which a new pharmacare program, which the New Democratic Party had introduced, was needed, and he was $100 million out.
People screamed "fiscal irresponsibility". They said, "You socialists can't run a peanut stand", but they elected a good number of government members in the next federal election when the country was running an $11 billion deficit. The government buried $100 million in the ground at Pickering. No one will ever see that money again. The government squandered millions of dollars on the Mirabel airport.
It becomes a question of trying to understand the difference between a million and a billion. Many people do not quite understand the difference in the amounts, but we cannot continue to operate government irrationally, and we cannot continue to provide the services the public demands. It is not just this party which demands additions to welfare, additions to pensions, and further government interference in the area of welfare. That has generally been popular and will continue to be popular. However, with this kind of deficit financing, the hands of any government will be tied when it tries to improve that particular feature.

One of the reasons for this bill is the fact that we are now wasting as much as $1 million a day abroad to buttress the value of the Canadian dollar. I have seen figures ranging from $750,000 to $1 million a day. Surely that is the most monumental waste of all. People can talk all they like about civil servants who have not been earning their salaries, allegedly, etc., but that $1 million a day is a phenomenal waste.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) tells us that our trade picture is improving and that in fact we in this country are getting out from under, but the reality is that we are continuing to go in the wrong direction. It is not the trade picture which is causing the Canadian dollar to fall and fall. In 1977 we had a surplus on the merchandise trade account of something close to $3 billion, but when we look at our service transactions and examine what we have paid in travel, interest, dividends, freight, shipping and other areas, the key figure lies in what we are paying out to those who have lent money to Canada both privately and publicly. That figure is just about $3.5 billion a year, and it is a drain on the resources of this country.
The trend I have seen in this House is that foreign ownership is no longer an issue and that we are so desperate for capital that we do not need to review foreign investment seriously. We have the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and we have a minister who really is acting like a fox among the chickens.
There is no question that our free trader Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has no real interest in controlling foreign investment or directing it only to those areas which are in desperate need. A classic example in my own province is what happened in the fishing industry.
As a result of negotiations at the Law of the Sea Conference-and I might say that the Canadian delegation played a vital and constructive role in them-we have expanded our sea boundaries out to 200 miles. The result, however, is that Japan is the big loser. The Japanese desperately need fishing markets where they can get fish to continue to supply the massive Japanese fish market. Therefore they have placed capital on the market in that industry which is more advantageous to us than capital we can get anywhere else. They have said that they want a piece of our fishing action so that they can be guaranteed access to that resource. I have every sympathy for Japan in doing that, but I have no sympathy for a government which does not understand what Japan is trying to accomplish. This means that jobs are going to Japan. It means that we do not process our fish here, and it also means that the price of that product can be artificially depressed where purchase agreements are tied to loans to the Canadian fishing industry.
Because of a lack of imagination on the part of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce we are allowing foreign capital to come into our fishing industry without restriction or review. As a matter of fact, it is not reviewable because it is loan capital. It is not take-over capital, and it is not establishing new industry. We do not have legislation to control it. A government with imagination would not allow this to happen but, rather than taking the draconian move of saying we will
October 20, 1978

not allow capital-and clearly the fishing industry needs capital-we should be saying that we will offer Canadian capital at better rates than the Japanese are offering it.
We should go to that market and say that if it needs capital it must get Canadian capital and that it will get Canadian capital at better than competitive rates. That is only one example of what could be done if we had a government with an industrial strategy. This government has none. It continues to operate on a day to day basis, and it looks like that day to day operation will be coming to an end in the near future. That might not be a bad thing.
It might be a good thing to have a change of government, whether it be a change to a Conservative government or to a New Democratic Party government. I think a change may be necessary to get the spirit of this country going again, because there has been an atmosphere of tiredness for a long time in terms of the way our affairs have been conducted.
We talk a lot about economic conditions in Canada. We hear much rhetoric in this place and in politics generally to the effect that everything which happens in the country is the direct result of whatever government may happen to be in power. While the New Democratic Party was in office in British Columbia between 1974 and 1975 there was a total of 100 bankruptcies. The following year there was a total of 197. In the following year there was a change of government. The new government said that the New Democratic Party had been scaring foreign capital away, that it was far too tough on the business community and that it was in fact antagonistic to the business community. In the first year of office of the new government the number of bankruptcies rose to 421, and in 1977-78 the number rose to 674. In the first five months of this year there were 281 bankruptcies.
I am not saying that that is the fault of the provincial government nor the fault of the federal government, and I am not saying that there were no bankruptcies or very few in British Columbia when there was a socialist government, or because there was a socialist government. These things occur from time to time in the cyclical economy we have, and people who are engaged in the field of politics have great difficulty restraining their rhetoric. Blame is always cast as if all the evils of the world sit right at the government's door, and it is said that the new Jerusalem will come when we change governments. That is not going to happen. We are faced with certain realities, and no matter which government we have, that government will have to embrace the concept that in the world of the future there will be less to distribute.
Now, I happen to think that the NDP, or democratic socialism, is the best vehicle to have as a government when a crisis exists and when one has to consider the possibility of future scarcity in the world, it is only the NDP, with its principle of equality in sharing, which can hold the political fabric together. Because in the long run, over the years, we have developed a welfare state in Canada, and we have always congratulated ourselves around the world that somehow we are
Borrowing Authority Act
very fine people because we have been redistributing wealth and we have been creating old age pensions, unemployment insurance, and the various other social programs. The reality is that the people of Canada have given nothing to those particular projects, nor have the governments.
What has happened is that our economy has expanded and we have taken the additional wealth we have created and redistributed a little bit of it. But no one else has said, "I am taking less". People out there have said, "We want more, more and more". All I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that the day will come when we will not be able to do that any more, when someone will have to make a sacrifice, when the spirit that was abroad in this country in the second world war will have to come back, and when we will be willing to give and to sacrifice.
The reality is that in the last ten years the poor section of the population has retained approximately the same percentage of the GNP, about 4 per cent, and the rich, the top 10 per cent, have retained something in the order of 20 per cent of the wealth. There has been no redistribution of wealth, and we have created our social programs out of the expansion of the pie. The proposition is that, if that pie stops expanding, we will have serious trouble in this country because someone will have to give up something, and that has not been the case up to now. There has been enough to distribute and, I suggest, only the philosophy of democratic socialism can contemplate that particular crisis which we might have in the future.
Now, what is the immediate solution to the question of the dollar? The idea that we should continue to allow the natural flow of capital to take place between Canada and the rest of the world is a disastrous mistake in terms of the dollar. Unless the government has the courage to impose some kind of exchange controls, problems that we have seen in such places as Sudbury, problems that we have seen where it is far more advantageous to invest in the resource sector of the third world, will continue to exist. We cannot allow the drain of Canadian capital to continue.
I am not suggesting that exchange controls need to be applied on small amounts of money leaving this country, but let us take a figure in the area of, say, $75,000. You might then say that the Parliament of Canada believes that you should keep your money in Canada, that Canada is still a capital shy country but it is particularly capital shy in terms of Canadian capital. If we do not impose some exchange controls, the dollar will continue to be soft at 84 cents or 85 cents-it could even go lower.
I do not suspect that this particular bill will do much for the Canadian dollar. I suppose that the people who look at money in the city of New York are looking at this piece of legislation to borrow another $7 billion abroad wondering what will happen to the Canadian dollar after it is passed. Exchange controls are the immediate answer to two major problems: the first is the softness in the Canadian dollar; and the second, and perhaps the most important one, is that the multinationals which have come to Canada, which have reaped the benefits of our resources, which have made some contribution to this

What we do with bad citizens is to pass laws to place some kind of control on them, and until we take courage in our hands and impose exchange controls on the capital flows of multinational corporations, Sudbury will just be the beginning of a massive problem all across our resource sector. As a matter of fact I do not think that companies like Cominco and some of our pulp and paper giants would be unsympathetic to a temporary exchange control once the total problem was explained to them, and once they understood the difficult situation in which this country has now been placed as a result of the movement of the capital that has accumulated in this country.
There is too often a simplicity in the debate in this place. All too often unnecessary cheap shots and slanging matches between members of parliament take place here, and 1 want to tell you that the public does not appreciate that at all. I think they are tired of the stupidity of debate in this place, they are tired of personalities jumping up and throwing jibes at each other. I do not think that kind of conduct enhances this place or enhances the reputation of politics or politicians. It is time we in the House ended the personality conflicts and got down to talking about issues, instead of, "What did you do at some time in the past", etc., etc.

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in his initial speech commencing debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Yesterday the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the financial critic for the opposition, identified the countries as being West Germany, the United States, Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland, and one or two other places and then I referred to the point originally raised by the hon. Leader of the Opposition, which was reiterated yesterday by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, that Canada was in seventh place in relation to these countries. They both indicated that Canadians were sitting on a tier which was seven points down in relation to some other western industrialized countries.
I raised the point yesterday that that was completely incorrect. I referred to statistics of four and five years ago, statistics regarding increases in food prices, employment records, creation of new jobs, housing starts and a number of other areas. Also I pointed out that Canada was in second place in most of these cases, and that some of the countries mentioned by the hon. member for York-Simcoe as being in a far better position than Canada were in fact as low down as fourteenth, fifteenth, or in a number of cases, eighth, ninth or tenth place as compared to this country. I made that point yesterday and I might come back to a few more of these statistics this afternoon.
I should like at this time to come back to a quote that was said to come from the hon. member for York-Simcoe, the financial critic for the opposition, on a commentary on the radio this morning, in which the inference was left, with me at least as an early morning listener of early news broadcast, I think it was at seven o'clock, that Canadians were building for themselves debt upon debt which they are going to have a great deal of trouble paying back. I think that was the context

of his remarks; at least, that was the inference I gained from the point made by the newscaster.
I believe the hon. member was comparing our situation with that of the United States. That is probably a reasonable comparison in view of the fact that we do compare so much of what we do in this country with what is done in the United States. The U.S. is our best customer and is where 70 per cent of our exports go and, contrary to what former President Nixon thought, we all know Canada is in turn its best customer. I think he thought at one time that Japan was, but that impression was soon corrected. We are, indeed, each other's best customer, so I think a reasonable comparison would be the long-term debt outstanding of the two countries.
The comparison I want to make is in terms of the borrowings outstanding by the two countries; that is, by the central governments in Washington and Ottawa. This is again in relation to gross national product. In other words, these are percentages of gross national product. I will go first to the period from 1960 to 1969 in order that we get a little bit of the history of a period during which, at least for a few years, this country was governed by that party on the other side of the House one of the few periods in this century when they have had the opportunity of being the government.
The figure for the United States during that period is 39.2 per cent. That is the percentage of the U.S. gross national product, for a given year, that is represented by their total outstanding debt. That figure has come down over the years in the United States, from 1960 to 1969 to the year 1977. The United States has improved the situation to the point that this figure now stands at only 29.9 per cent of the gross national product, represented by total outstanding debt. That is the long-term debt owed by the central government, and indirectly owed by every resident of the U.S.A. Those are the American figures.
The Canadian figures are amazingly close for the period 1960 to 1969, in fact varying by one-tenth of 1 per cent. In that period the central government debt in Canada, which is the federal government debt, was 39.3 per cent of our gross national product, as against the United States figure of 39.2 per cent. As I say, with one-tenth of 1 per cent variation, basically the two are identical.
We move to 1977. I mentioned earlier that the United States seemed to have improved its situation in that the total long-term debt outstanding decreased as a percentage of gross national product. I think the variation in the United States was some 12 percentage points. The same thing happened in Canada. This is not going to be happy news for members of the opposition, because again it is a little bit of good financial news. actual costs. These are good figures and that is why we do not hear very much about them, unfortunately.
The figure has come down from 39.3 per cent for the period 1960-69 to 27.4 per cent for 1977. I mentioned earlier that the United States had brought its figure down to 29.9 per cent, whereas ours is 27.4 per cent. That is a considerably better performance than occurred in the United States.
In other words, 27.4 per cent of our gross national product today is the figure that is represented by our total central government outstanding debt. In comparison, the U.S. figure is 29.9 per cent. In other words, Canadians do not owe as much as Americans in terms of our total outstanding central government debt in relation to gross national product, which is the product of all our goods and services produced in any one year.
This is a far cry from the hon. member's insinuation. Indeed, it is more than an insinuation; it is in fact a direct comment broadcast on our national news service to all Canadians as they got up for breakfast this morning, and emanated from the speech made by the financial critic and senior financial spokesman of the opposition party in this House yesterday, in probably his first major speech this session on a financial bill. In introducing Bill C-7 the minister set forth very clearly the purposes of the bill. From listening to the debate one would think there was something insidious about this bill. In fact there is not. It is a very routine bill. It is the type of bill put before the House of Commons quite frequently which quite often passes without a great deal of difficulty or long debate.
At this particular time the official opposition sees some advantage in making a political football out of this bill. We have listened to all kinds of red herrings in this debate. No one in this House can do that more capably than the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). In listening to him today he took us all the way from the time of his great-grandparents to the present. He brought in the old red herring which the Tories are using more and more nowadays and which some of their candidates used in the by-elections. As well, some Tory premiers and Tory hopefuls are using this same red herring in provincial elections. It is the so-called issued of the removal of the powers from the Queen. If they do not know it, that is an absolute fabrication and they should stop using it because it is damaging not only to the Queen but to the country.
It has been clearly stated in the government bill introduced for the purposes of discussion and creating interest in the issue of constitutional reform that the government does not intend now, did not intend in the past nor does intend in the future, to remove or lessen the powers of the Queen.
Ever since 1215 the power of the British monarchy has steadily and progressively diminished, until today we have a parliamentary democracy in which there is very little power given to the monarchy. However, there are some potent prerogatives which our present Queen is free to exercise and which have not been removed or diminished by this government, nor will they be. As a result I find it offensive that the official opposition tries to mislead the public by bringing in that kind of argument in discussing bills which are totally unrelated to the situation. I am not trying to claim that the government should not be subject to criticism from the opposition; obviously that is the role of the opposition. But it would be refreshing if at least once in a while there was some constructive criticism coming from the other side, particularly the official opposition.
On the other hand, I must compliment the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). The speech he made this afternoon was constructive. It was not designed to destroy but
October 20, 1978

to criticize in a constructive way. I say that whether or not members agree with what the hon. member said, but his remarks were made in a positive manner.
I am also concerned with the charges and counter-charges made in this House and the effect they will have on our nation in the days and years ahead. We are living in a time when there are those who doubt very seriously the future of our country as a unified nation consisting of two founding races and many other ethnic groups. I wonder what purpose is being served in continually trying to downgrade our country by saying that everything is bad. If one listens to the official opposition everything is worse than it has ever been, and that it is worse in Canada than it is in almost any other country. Everything is put in the negative superlative in order to try to score some political points. In my opinion that will not serve the interests of our nation.
We have heard a lot of figures which have been bandied about across the floor in the last few days on the relative standing of Canada vis-a-vis other nations of the world. Peculiar uses have been made of these figures in trying to show that Canada is just on the verge of bankruptcy. As well these figures have been used to try to show that the citizens of Canada are suffering irreparable economic harm, and that that economic harm is increasing day by day. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is not true.
I ask the opposition, how many of them would prefer to live in one of the countries that they are holding up as examples to us? How many of them would prefer to live in one of those countries rather than in Canada? How many of them would prefer to buy their groceries in West Germany rather than in Canada? How many of them would prefer to buy their petroleum in Great Britain rather than in Canada? How many of them would prefer to buy their clothing in any of the countries making up the European Common Market? In other words, how many of them would like to take the income of people in any of the other industrialized nations of the world and have to support themselves in those nations? How many of them would honestly say they would prefer that and that they would be better off than they are living in Canada? I do not hear any answers.
The bill before the House requests authority to borrow. As I said, it is not an unusual bill. It specifically requests authority to borrow $7 billion for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1979, and borrowing authority to a total of $10 billion for the fiscal year 1979-1980. That, of course, does not mean all of that money will necessarily be borrowed, but it means the authority has been given by parliament to the government to borrow those sums if it becomes necessary.
We have already been told that the cash requirements for
1977-	1978 were $8.3 billion and the cash requirements for
1978-	79 will be $11.8 billion. That is a total of $20.1 billion for two years plus U.S. exchange loans of $750 million and other borrowings of 1.5 million Deutschmarks. It is conceivable that other lines of credit will have to be arranged or other borrowings made in order to ensure that the position of the

This is not an unusual bill. I am therefore surprised that the opposition is trying to make a political football of it. I simply want to put on record today my view that, despite the political atmosphere in the country at the moment, it behooves us all to speak with care and attention when dealing with the economy of our nation. I do not think it serves the purpose of our government, the opposition nor our nation to continue to try and score political points at the expense of our nation's economy.

In fact, what happens is that those

What happens, Mr. Speaker, in cases such as what was reported this week is that action is being taken to sell our products to distant countries. In order to do that we must have the necessary funds to encourage companies which may be new in Canada and not in a position to take the risk. Of course it means that the Canadian government must offer guarantees and insurance so that these companies can recognize that when they do sell abroad they will be paid, independently of the buyer's ability to honour his obligations.
