There were questions raised regarding the financing and the capital structure of Petro-Canada, because there has to be a great deal of investment in energy resources if we are going to ensure supplies for a long period of time. In order to finance that kind of investment we have to borrow, which is perhaps one of the reasons why on a regular basis we present borrowing bills to this House. In case hon. members opposite get sensitive about what Petro-Canada has to do with this borrowing bill, I simply point out that in order to invest moneys we have to borrow from time to time so that we can secure a return on our investment at some future time.
There is no question but that Petro-Canada is our window into the petro-chemical industry. The United States is the only major oil producer in the world which does not have a national petroleum corporation. Mexico has one, Indonesia has one, Nigeria has one, the OPEC countries have one and Venezuela has one. There is a recognition that what is contained under the ground in Saskatchewan really belongs to the people. It does not belong to the fellow who is lucky enough to find it. He should, of course, get a fair return, there is no question about that; but the wealth that is under the ground should belong to the people collectively.

It might be difficult for people in the country to understand the nature of this debate. It is not a debate about a specific borrowing taking place. It is a debate about the actual authority and the limit on it which is maintained over the years in order that a parliamentary procedure may take place before additional authority is given. Obviously the authority required for a government in any circumstances is enough to deal with the issues it faces in borrowing and also enough to provide for contingencies so that it may be in a position to take reasonable steps to deal with financial emergencies and foreign exchange activities which might arise. It is, therefore, the amount of authority required to meet governing problems.
What is extraordinary here is that presumably the official opposition, in putting forward their amendment, would vote to curtail this authority of the government, although they themselves know that such authority is required in today's circumstances. It is required in part to deal with budget deficits and in part to deal with matters in the world of exchange where both the U.S. and the Canadian dollar are seriously under attack. I say the Canadian and U.S. dollar because, of course, many people believe that the Canadian dollar is affected by what happens to the U.S. dollar, regardless of what we might do inside our country. This bill could have supplied the specific total amount now for this year to deal with contingencies a year and a half or so ahead. Instead it does it in two stages so as to specify that, in the current fiscal year, no more than $7 billion of that authority will be sought to be used, and therefore it is not requested.

This afternoon we heard an excellent speech by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), a member of the New Democratic Party. I regret to hear that he is not planning to seek re-election. His speech was excellent in almost every regard, but I have to reserve my position on his comment that he was not sure if his party would vote against the authority being sought in the bill because of the extent of the borrowing request for next year. He said that on the ground that sooner or later there should be some balanced budgets. I agree with him on that, but surely he would agree that the "sooner or later" will not happen next year in this country. Given all we can project regarding present economic conditions, the situation next year certainly will require a significant deficit again.
For several years now the government has been engaged in a cost cutting exercise, an exercise of retraint in its spending, in limiting growth in the public service, and in cutting back the number of man-years employed. It is not a new venture on our part. When we engaged in it, we knew as we began that it was not an easy exercise. It was an exercise of finding out in various parts of big government operation where things can be done more efficiently, more effectively, and then examine them again as to their efficiency and effectiveness.
It is an ongoing job which in one sense should always continue. In the last three years we have undertaken it with zeal. That is why our situation is so different from that which faced the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) when he was prime minister. He entered the debate today, perhaps stung by the memory of the fact that once before in the country when the dollar was falling he was prime minister and found it impossible to escape the blame and criticism for the economic conditions which brought that about.
The difference is that in the late 1950s and early 1960s, the government of the day was in circumstances where the hon. member for New Westminster, had he been in the House then,

would have called for economic responsibility and a sign of a government in control of a situation. Instead he would have found the Diefenbaker government spending irresponsibly and exercising no restraint whatever. In those days when the dollar suffered because of lack of confidence in the economy as a result of government action, naturally blame was attached immediately to the government of the day.
It should be noted to some extent the government will fall heir to the spirit of criticism which existed in those days. However, the situation is very signficantly different. Even with the restraint we have been exercising for three years in regard to government spending, and the responsibility we have been showing, time after time the opposition thought we were in a pre-election period and expected us to go to the limit in terms of spending and minimizing taxation. Instead, we produced three budgets which were criticized by the official opposition for not having enough spending and too much taxing. The official opposition, budget after budget, has asserted that our deficits should be larger than they have been. That is a sign of the responsibility of the government.
Our dollar is under attack, as is the American dollar, in a world where certain things fundamentally have changed, oil prices being one of them. Canada has its own special factors which cause a problem for the dollar. In terms of investor confidence, as misplaced as it may be to argue that a separatist government has created threat to the country and its unity, that is without a doubt one factor. It is not a factor investors should take into account, but it is one which is often subtle when looked at by would-be investors, and leads to judgments as to where investments should take place. It is apparent a good amount of Canadian money is going abroad to be invested, rather than simply a lack of foreign money coming here. That is where it becomes important to re-emphasize at every turn the reasons why Canada and Canadians ought to have absolute, firm confidence in the future of the country and its economic development.
Of course, the opposition must, as part of its natural objectives create as much doom and gloom about the future as possible. As a government, we must challenge that and emphasize why Canadians should have confidence in their future and in the actions of the government in relation to the constitution, language, and questions which otherwise might feed separatism.
The government has been successful to such a degree that that threat should not be considered real or realistic in the minds of investors, subject to the continuation of the type of leadership displayed by the government. The fact of the matter is that the Canadian economy is buoyant and strong. More jobs are being created in Canada each year than in any other area of the world, relative to the nature of the economy and the size of the country. Year after year we have seen jobs created in numbers which outpace the proportionate increase in population. If in a 12-month period the number of new jobs is 375,000 higher,iris well out of proportion to the increase in population during that period. If in a ten-year period the increase in jobs is two million, when a population increase of
October 20, 1978

three million has occurred, then clearly more Canadians in proportion to the population are working at paying jobs and more Canadians are supporting the economy with these jobs than ever before.
We should not let ourselves be misled by the existence at the same time of even a larger number of people seeking work. As a government we are not misled. We know the economy is strong, but we are not misled by the fact that additional efforts must be put to the task of assuring that work is found for those who want it. Even though we expressed satisfaction with the increase in the number of jobs, we are not satisfied about the amount of unemployment and the challenge for additional jobs. We continue to turn our attention to that in economic measures, job-creation measures, industrial incentives measures, and throughout our government of this country.
Behind the unemployment figures we realize, if the official opposition does not, there is a chronic situation, as well as the current one of a lot of people wanting jobs. The chronic problem is that of a very large number of people seeking jobs without jobs to be found for them in the eastern part of the country, from Montreal to the east, throughout a good part of Quebec and the whole of the Atlantic region.
It is for that reason that this government has made effort after effort to try to strengthen and expand the efforts of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and has tailored its unemployment programs, its employment-creating programs and its Canada Works program toward assisting the eastern region of the country. I hope hon. members opposite support that effort to help these areas of the country where the problem is chronic.
Instead of supporting it, however, may I remind you again, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members in the Conservative party far too often attack these programs by relating them to assistance for Quebec in that very insidious way they have of ignoring the fact that, because the problem is even more serious in the Atlantic region, even more attention by us has been placed upon the Atlantic region in job-creation and regional development. That we will continue to do and we will continue to look for solutions. We do not say we have found all the answers. We believe, however, that we are facing up to the problem and recognizing it for what it is.
The economy of this country has faced for some years the challenge of inflation, and indeed, if there is one thing more than any other which can be identified as putting pressure on the Canadian dollar and forcing it down, it is inflation in this country, fired by demands for wages and other forms of return which are out of line with what can be expected, given the need to share some of the productivity gains, and given the cost to the world of rapid increases in energy prices. Whether it is foreign oil or increased prices for oil which give great returns to Alberta and Saskatchewan, for which I am naturally grateful as a prairie boy, the fact of the matter is that those returns have to be obtained from all Canadians.
Borrowing Authority Act
Those who ignored the fact that this was a cost we all had to share and tried, through increases in returns, in wages, profits or salaries, to obtain full recompense for productivity increases and cost of living increases, are the people who tried to move the load of inflation and energy price increases to those who are not protected and cannot protect themselves.
This government, remaining true to its Liberal principles, took steps in these difficult economic times where inflation was a challenge to make sure that those who suffer most from these forms of attack by inflation were helped. That is why we have announced new funds for those who have families and are in a low income position, and it is why we have announced a $20 increase in the guaranteed income supplement for those who are retired and depend upon the old age pension and the income supplement for their livelihood. These are Liberal principles applied at a time when our own policy has been for three years one of stern spending restraint, and at a time when we are facing a budget deficit which we believe is as much as it reasonably ought to be in the economic circumstances of the day.
This is a time when we are facing the need to find those funds and have put into place further spending cuts and the removal of programs, many of which we believe are good in themselves but which simply have to be put in a lower priority category compared to helping the family on low income and the elderly who depend upon the OAS and GIS for their sole support. This also meant we had to cut some programs in order to find funds for the industrial incentive programs we have already put forward and will be putting forward in the House.
We have not decided to go to a larger deficit for these matters because of our challenge in respect of inflation, a challenge we continue to face and are going to have to face by encouraging all Canadians to examine the question of restraint in their own demands upon the economy. Yet we are faced with an opposition which says we should spend more, tax less and have a larger deficit, but should not have the authority to borrow the funds which we would obviously require if the deficit were larger.
That is an irresponsibility from an opposition whose members think they can get away with it because the issue is complex and the people may not understand. I think gradually and over time people have a very shrewd way of judging these irresponsible approaches to economic management, and I think they will so judge the official opposition as well.
The last factor I should like to refer to in this approach by the official opposition is its recent proposal for mortgage deductions from income, which every commentator has seen as being a forgiveness of tax to the rich much more than to the poor. It excludes whole classes of people, including particularly the elderly who own homes free of mortgage. This is a program which will mean a loss of $1.6 billion in revenue for the treasury. It will cost even more when the program works its way through and people take on mortgages to get the benefit of the proposal, as we have seen happen in the United States. The opposition puts this proposal forward without saying what it will do to replace that loss of $1.6 billion in

October 20, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
revenue, or what it will do about the further taxation it will have to impose to balance the budget or to hold the deficit in line with current thinking. That is again an irresponsibility which we will, over the coming months, have to point out clearly to the people of Canada.
Even more than that, I think our real challenge as a government and as a people is not only to continue to grapple with the problem of inflation which is fired by excessive demand, as well as grapple with the problem of chronic unemployment in areas like Quebec and Atlantic Canada, but also to inspire once again confidence among Canadians in the fact that our economy is, indeed, very strong; that in every sector, except those we have had to help because they could not help themselves, real incomes are better than they were before. This is measured in terms of disposable income and savings, and measured in terms which are very visible at airports and railway stations and by those who organize charters abroad. All of this shows that we Canadians are clearly better off than ever before.
The one thing that is lacking is clear confidence in our future. There is no reality in fact for that lack of confidence, and we recognize the challenge to restore it. Because if one thing more than another is needed in addition to restraint on a government that has committed itself, it is restraint on demand for higher wages, salaries and profits. We must find ways of getting Canadians to accept this fact in the absence of a wage and price control program.
One additional thing needed is for Canadians to readdress themselves to the fact that this country is strong and vibrant, that they have been the recipients over time of Liberal policies and programs of many kinds to assist those who are in need and inspire economic growth, without attempting to override the private investment sector in so doing. People in Canada must, as I say, recognize that this country is strong and vibrant and that they should have faith in it. This will restore the flow of investment into this country and will be an important ingredient in dealing with the problems this country faces.

It is essential that the people of Canada understand the government's reasons for asking for this borrowing authority. It is not the borrowing itself that is important but the right for the rest of this fiscal year and throughout the next to borrow sums of money that may be required.
There are a couple of essential points that I would like to add to the understanding we have gained this afternoon. The first one is that this borrowing authority does not represent additional spending by the government in the rest of this fiscal year or the next. It would be a false impression to think that this borrowing was for something new, something not already divulged in the government's program.
The government over the past two years has made it very clear that its firm intention and its practice is to reduce government spending, and it is on course in that respect, not least of all in the announcement on August 1. The total requirements of this government are well known, and they do include a significant deficit this year and next year. There are reasons for those deficits. This borrowing authority is to provide a legal foundation for those deficits, and there are economic and fiscal reasons for doing so. We need to have the legal framework in which to do the borrowing to support those deficits.
A second reason for the borrowing is to bring the authority into line with the stand-by credit already negotiated.
A third reason for the borrowing authority, one that will be of interest to Canadians, is to protect the government's current cash reserves in Canadian dollars for the purchase of American dollars when our dollar rises again.
Why would this lead one to borrow? It is because we have acquired Canadian dollars in the process of the falling dollar as it sought the lower levels. Those dollars will be required again to purchase U.S. dollars as our dollar rises. If those dollars were spent in current operations or in investment in Canada's future, as in Central Mortgage and Housing mort-
October 20, 1978

gages or in Petro-Canada development in energy and so forth, we would subsequently have to borrow Canadian dollars to purchase U.S. dollars to replenish the reserves. Reserves go out and come back. Canadian dollars are purchased as they fall in value. American dollars are purchased as our dollar rises. Therefore, we want to save Canadian dollars for that return upward. Those are some of the reasons which make it prudent for the government at this time to seek from parliament the authority to borrow.
Is the Canadian debt of such unusual size that it would cause concern in the country? We do have Canadian government debt and it has risen substantially, like most things. Our incomes have risen, as has the value of Canada's production and our entire economy.
The most sensible way of responding to the question whether our debt is now really very high, and would these additions make it unusually high, is to make some comparisons.

Naturally, members of the opposition are going to say yes. I have a table which is an international comparison on public debt as reflected in the debt of central governments such as Great Britain, the United States, Germany, Canada, etc. As the hon. parliamentary secretary to the minister said in his excellent speech this afternoon-and I found it an instructive point-we should compare our Canadian government debt with the American government debt, take a look at what has been the trend to see whether we have diverged, whether we are out of line, or whether we think that their debt is excessively high.
The period for the 1960s shows that the Canadian government debt and the U.S. debt reflected the same percentage of their economic production in any one year. For example, about 39 per cent of our annual production would have paid off the debt in that one year, which means we had that kind of relationship to our total economy. It may be that the debt has doubled or tripled in certain periods, depending on the period you want to take, but the economy has doubled and tripled along with the debt.
It is only reasonable to ask, is the weight of the debt today heavier in the economy than it was back in the sixties? The answer is no; Canada's public debt as reflected by the Government of Canada's direct debt is a lesser burden on the Canadian economy in 1977, according to the last figures we have, by roughly 10 percentage points. That is 25 per cent less. I do not have the actual figures worked out, but it could be said that it would take a little over a quarter of our production to pay the total debt off.
Where do we stand with respect to the United States? In 1977 the United States had a central government debt representing 30 per cent of its gross national product for that year,

and 1 have rounded that figure; the actual figure was 29.9 per cent. The Canadian government's debt was less than the American in relation to its own economy. The figure for Canada was 27.4 per cent. Not only have we stayed generally in line with what is going on in the United States, but we have done a little better.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Why have we done a little better? It is not only that we have struggled to invest in the Canadian economy with government borrowing and investments, but that the Canadian economy has outperformed the American economy over those periods of years so that the debt we have is a lesser proportion of the total economy than it is in the American case.
I will not trouble the House at this late time in the afternoon with more statistics that would reflect the faster growth of the Canadian economy over the American economy, because those points were made today and yesterday quite clearly. I want to stress that one of the sources of growth in both economies, and indeed in all economies, is borrowings. Borrowing when seen from another direction is an investment in the future. Borrowing is not made for frivolous reasons. Money is borrowed to invest in a country's social structure and in its economic structure. Investments are made in education. Investments are made in things like Petro-Canada in order to discover new energy resources, particularly in the frontier regions where the cost of exploration and production will be very high.
We are investing in the rehabilitation of grain gathering railway lines in western Canada. That takes in a large sum of money. Borrowings support such investments. Borrowings such as those we are seeking authority for today help to rehabilitate western Canada's grain lines. That is one reason why the economy of Canada is outperforming other economies. We are making investments in restructuring so that revenues will come back later and less subsidies will be required.
Borrowings also go to rehabilitate the fishing harbours in Atlantic Canada. Why do I mention that? If we have the new 200-mile fishing zone off our shores on both coasts, we will have to provide bigger harbours for bigger boats that go out to catch the fish. We will have to invest in shipbuilding and we will have to provide better breakwaters than the old ones used for smaller boats. It is foolishness not to borrow to invest in that sort of future and have the borrowing paid off as taxes bring back funds to repay that debt.
I could go on and on. Such bodies as the Export Development Corporation, the CNR and Air Canada will be asked to borrow on their own, but we have been providing them with hundreds of millions of dollars. Is it fair to say to the taxpayers today: "You pay money in taxes and we will give it to the Export Development Corporation to lend to another country, so that the other country will buy our manufactured goods, our technology and our ability to build an airport for them and engage our engineers and so forth"? No, it is not fair to ask taxpayers, today to pay those taxes, because the returns come in over 20 years, 15 years, ten years. It is money borrowed.

Borrowing Authority Act
The authority we are now seeking from this parliament is the authority to continue to invest in an improved economy for the sake of those taxpayers ten years, 15 years and 20 years down the line. There is no question in my mind that we not only must continue that process-and these borrowings are for the rest of this year and all of next year-but that we will continue to get returns for it.
I would like to point out one other aspect of why borrowing authority is being sought. I refer to the rather unique spreading out of our revenues as a government and our expenditures as a government. Is anyone in the House going to object to the indexation of family allowance or unemployment insurance or senior citizen's pensions? That change was undertaken I believe in 1973, when the oil crisis sent inflation reverberations all over the world. We had to face those circumstances, and we said we would protect such people against inflation.
